name: Anton Tkáč
milestone_by_age_26: Won World Championship gold in match sprint at age 23 (1974) and Olympic gold in match sprint at age 25 (1976), defeating eight-time World Champion Daniel Morelon.
early_history_summary: Tkáč started as a track and field athlete at a sports school in Bratislava before turning to cycling at age 17, winning a recruitment race on a borrowed bike. He was recruited by the Slovan Bratislava cycling club and quickly rose through national championships, earning a World Championship nomination at 18 in 1969. After a disappointing 8th place, he intensified training and won bronze at the 1970 World Championship in Leicester at age 19.
family_context_summary: Born in Lozorno, a village near Bratislava, Czechoslovakia. Family background not documented in reviewed sources beyond his athletic upbringing in the state sports school system.
primary_early_advantage_tags: state sports school, Slovan Bratislava club, national team pipeline, coach Igor Stiassny, trained alongside Ondrej Nepela
evidence_summary: Tkáč benefited from the Czechoslovak state sports system, attending a sports school in Bratislava and being recruited to the Slovan Bratislava cycling club where trainer Igor Stiassny guided his early development. He trained alongside figure skating Olympic champion Ondrej Nepela at the same club. Despite severe injuries including a skull fracture, his intense training and physical talent propelled him to World Championship bronze at 19, gold at 23, and Olympic gold at 25. Family financial or domain background is not documented.
starting_point: Born in 1951 in Lozorno, a village near Bratislava, Czechoslovakia; family background not documented beyond attendance at a state sports school.
current_position: Died on December 22, 2022 in Bratislava at age 71 after a long illness; final role was sports administrator and former chairman of the Slovak Cycling Federation (2001–2011).

trajectory.event: Won bronze medal in the 1 km time trial at the World Championship in Leicester, missing silver by 0.02 seconds.
Won World Championship gold in match sprint in Montreal, his first world title.
Won Olympic gold medal in match sprint at the Montreal Olympics, defeating eight-time World Champion Daniel Morelon.
Won his second World Championship gold in match sprint in Munich.
Finished fourth at the Moscow Olympics and retired from competitive cycling.
Became chairman of the Slovak Cycling Federation, serving until 2011.
Died on December 22 in Bratislava after a long illness.

name: Igor Krutoy
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Krutoy's first major success came in 1987 at age 33 with the hit song 'Madonna' performed by Alexander Serov. By age 26 (1980), he had just started working as a pianist at the Moscow Concert Orchestra 'Panorama'.
early_history_summary: Krutoy taught himself accordion as a child in Haivoron, Ukraine, and graduated from Kirovograd Music College in 1974. He failed to enter the Kiev Conservatory, taught music in a rural school, then studied at Nikolaev State Pedagogical Institute, graduating in 1979. He worked in restaurants and met singer Aleksander Serov, who would later perform his songs.
family_context_summary: Born to Jewish parents in Haivoron, Kirovograd Oblast, Ukrainian SSR. Father worked as an expediter at a radio parts factory and mother was a lab technician at a sanitary-epidemiological station.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources as having a musical family background; Krutoy taught himself accordion.
evidence_summary: Krutoy's early career was marked by persistent but modest musical education: self-taught accordion, music college in Kirovograd, a failed Conservatory attempt, and a pedagogical institute degree. His breakthrough came at age 33 in 1987 with the hit 'Madonna.' No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Elena Andreicheva
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Andreicheva began working in TV documentary production in 2006 (around age 22) but her Oscar-winning documentary was released in 2019 when she was approximately 36. The CSV lists birth_year as 2000, but all sources confirm she was born in 1984.
early_history_summary: Born in Kyiv, Ukraine, Andreicheva moved to the UK at age 11. She studied physics at Imperial College London (BSc 2005) and Science Communication (MSci 2006). She began working in TV documentary production in 2006, starting as a research assistant and assistant director.
family_context_summary: Born and partly raised in Kyiv, Ukraine, before moving to the UK at age 11. Her father had film cameras she enjoyed using as a child. Family financial background not documented.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources beyond mention of father's film cameras.
evidence_summary: Andreicheva's career began with university education at Imperial College London followed by entry-level TV documentary work from 2006. Her major milestone, winning the Academy Award for Best Documentary Short Subject, came in 2020 at approximately age 36. No material milestone by age 26 was identified.

name: Francesco Moser
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Girobio (amateur Giro d'Italia) at age 20 in 1971, turned professional in 1973, won Giro di Lombardia at 24 in 1975, and won the World Road Racing Championship at age 26 in 1977.
early_history_summary: Moser grew up on a family farm in Val di Cembra, Trentino, using bicycles daily to navigate steep vineyard terrain. He left school at 14 and worked the farm for four years before focusing on cycling at 18. He was the most gifted of four cycling Moser brothers (Aldo, Enzo, Diego) and won the amateur Giro d'Italia in 1971 before turning professional in 1973.
family_context_summary: Born in Palù di Giovo, a village near Trento in northern Italy. Grew up on a family farm in Val di Cembra, working in vineyards from age 14. The family used bicycles for daily transport around the estate.
parent_family_domain_summary: Moser came from a family of cyclists: his three older brothers Aldo, Enzo, and Diego were all professional cyclists. His nephew Moreno Moser also became a professional racer.
primary_early_advantage_tags: family of cyclists, three professional cyclist brothers, farm labor physical conditioning, Italian cycling culture, Trentino region
evidence_summary: Moser's early advantage was deeply rooted in his family: three older brothers were professional cyclists, providing direct domain mentorship and a cycling-native environment. Growing up on a steep vineyard farm built exceptional physical strength through manual labor, and daily bicycle use for farm transport gave him organic domain proximity. The Italian professional cycling ecosystem and his brothers' network facilitated his rapid rise from amateur Giro winner at 20 to professional at 22 to World Champion at 26.
starting_point: Born in 1951 in Palù di Giovo near Trento, Italy; grew up on a family farm in Val di Cembra where his father worked vineyards and the family used bicycles for daily transport.
current_position: Retired former professional cyclist with 273 career road victories; runs F Moser Bikes brand; resides in Trentino, Italy; estimated net worth not documented.

trajectory.event: Won the Girobio (amateur Giro d'Italia), establishing himself as a rising talent.
Competed in the individual road race and team time trial at the Munich Olympics.
Turned professional with Filotex team and won his first Giro d'Italia stage.
Won the Giro di Lombardia, his first Monument classic victory.
Won the World Road Racing Championship in San Cristobal, Venezuela.
Won the first of three consecutive Paris-Roubaix victories (1978, 1979, 1980).
Won the Giro d'Italia overall and broke Eddy Merckx's hour record in Mexico City.
Retired from professional cycling with 273 road victories, third all-time behind Merckx and Van Looy.

name: Jan A. P. Kaczmarek
milestone_by_age_26: Founded the Orchestra of the Eighth Day in 1977 at age 24, an experimental music ensemble that toured Europe in the late 1970s, and was a five-time winner of the Jazz Forum magazine poll during this period.
early_history_summary: Kaczmarek studied music from an early age in Konin, Poland, composing his school's anthem and music for theatrical productions in high school. Though he graduated with a law degree from Adam Mickiewicz University in Poznań in 1977, he abandoned a planned diplomatic career to compose music for Jerzy Grotowski's experimental Theater Laboratory, founding the Orchestra of the Eighth Day that same year.
family_context_summary: Born into a musically inclined family in Konin, Poland. His grandfather played live music for silent films, and Kaczmarek learned piano during childhood.
parent_family_domain_summary: Grandfather was a musician who played live music for silent films; family was musically inclined, though not professionally established in music.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Grotowski Theater Laboratory, Orchestra of the Eighth Day, Jazz Forum poll winner, Poznan avant-garde scene, musical grandfather
evidence_summary: Kaczmarek's early career was shaped by his connection to Jerzy Grotowski's innovative Theater Laboratory in Poznań, one of the most influential experimental theater centers in the world. He founded the Orchestra of the Eighth Day in 1977 at age 24, touring Europe and winning Jazz Forum magazine polls five times. His grandfather's musical background provided early exposure, and his law studies at Adam Mickiewicz University gave him intellectual breadth. His Oscar win for Finding Neverland came much later in 2005.
starting_point: Born in 1953 in Konin, Poland, into a musically inclined family; grandfather played live music for silent films, and Kaczmarek learned piano in childhood.
current_position: Died on May 21, 2024 in Kraków at age 71 after suffering from Multiple System Atrophy; final achievements included Oscar win for Finding Neverland (2005) and founding the Transatlantyk Festival and Rozbitek Institute.

trajectory.event: Founded the Orchestra of the Eighth Day and began working with Jerzy Grotowski's Theater Laboratory in Poznań.
Touring Europe with the Orchestra of the Eighth Day and winning Jazz Forum magazine poll as composer/performer.
Released first album 'Music for the End' on Flying Fish Records in the United States.
Relocated to Los Angeles to pursue international film composition career.
Won the Drama Desk Award for Outstanding Music in a Play for 'Tis Pity She's a Whore' off-Broadway.
Won the Academy Award for Best Original Score for Finding Neverland.
Died on May 21 in Kraków after a long struggle with Multiple System Atrophy.

name: May-Louise Flodin
milestone_by_age_26: Won Miss World 1952 at age 18, becoming the second Miss World winner and achieving the first back-to-back victory for Sweden in the pageant's history.
early_history_summary: Flodin was born in Stockholm, Sweden, and won the Miss World 1952 pageant on November 14, 1952 in London at age 18, representing Sweden. She was crowned by her predecessor Kiki Håkansson, also from Sweden, marking the first back-to-back victory in Miss World history. Little is documented about her life before or after the pageant.
family_context_summary: Born in Stockholm, Sweden. Family background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Miss World pageant, physical beauty, Swedish pageant tradition, post-war pageant boom
evidence_summary: Flodin won Miss World 1952 at age 18, a milestone driven primarily by physical appearance in the context of the post-war beauty pageant boom. Sweden had won the inaugural Miss World in 1951, and Flodin's victory continued that tradition. Very little is documented about her family background, training, or life after the pageant. She had three children and died in Stockholm in 2011.
starting_point: Born in 1934 in Stockholm, Sweden; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Died on February 4, 2011 in Stockholm at age 76; had three children; later life details sparsely documented.

trajectory.event: Won Miss World 1952 on November 14 in London, becoming the second Miss World winner and achieving Sweden's first back-to-back victory.
Died on February 4 in Stockholm, Sweden.

name: Herman Van Springel
milestone_by_age_26: Won Gent-Wevelgem at age 23 in 1966, finished 2nd in the Tour de France at age 25 in 1968 (one of the closest finishes in Tour history), and won Giro di Lombardia at 25 in 1968.
early_history_summary: Van Springel was born in Ranst, Belgium, and grew up in Grobbendonk in the Flemish Campine region. He turned professional in 1965 at age 22 with the Dr Mann team. In his first full season as a professional, he won Gent-Wevelgem in 1966, attacking on the descent of the Kemmelberg alongside some of cycling's biggest names. By 1968, he nearly won the Tour de France, losing to Jan Janssen in the final time trial by seconds.
family_context_summary: Born in Ranst, Belgium, and grew up in Grobbendonk in the Flemish Campine (Kempen) region. Family background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Flemish cycling heartland, Belgian professional cycling ecosystem, riding against Merckx and Anquetil, time trial specialization, Kempen region
evidence_summary: Van Springel's early advantage was rooted in growing up in the Flemish Campine region of Belgium, one of the world's most intense cycling cultures. He turned professional at 22 and immediately competed against legends like Eddy Merckx, Jacques Anquetil, and Rik Van Looy. His natural time-trialling ability and the Belgian professional cycling infrastructure propelled him to major wins by 23 and a near-Tour de France victory at 25. Family background is not documented.
starting_point: Born in 1943 in Ranst, Belgium; grew up in Grobbendonk in the Flemish Campine region, a heartland of Belgian cycling culture.
current_position: Died on August 25, 2022 in Grobbendonk at age 79 after a battle with a brain tumor; final career achievements included 7 Bordeaux-Paris victories and the nickname 'Monsieur Bordeaux-Paris.'

trajectory.event: Turned professional with the Dr Mann team, beginning a 17-year professional career.
Won Gent-Wevelgem, attacking on the Kemmelberg descent to claim his biggest win to date.
Finished 2nd in the Tour de France, losing to Jan Janssen in the final time trial by seconds; also won Giro di Lombardia and Omloop Het Volk.
Won the first of seven Bordeaux-Paris titles and the Grand Prix des Nations.
Won Paris-Nice and finished 2nd in the Giro d'Italia.
Retired from professional cycling after winning his seventh Bordeaux-Paris.
Died on August 25 in Grobbendonk after a battle with a brain tumor.

name: Marie-Theres Nadig
milestone_by_age_26: Won two Olympic gold medals (downhill and giant slalom) at the 1972 Sapporo Winter Olympics at age 17, defeating favorite Annemarie Moser-Pröll, and was named Swiss Sportswoman of the Year.
early_history_summary: Nadig was born in Flums, Switzerland, and joined the Skiclub Flumserberg. She won the giant slalom at the Swiss Junior National Championships in 1970 at age 16, made her World Cup debut in 1971 with a sixth-place finish in downhill, and achieved her first World Cup podium (second in downhill) less than a month before the 1972 Olympics. At 17, she stunned the skiing world by winning two Olympic golds in Sapporo.
family_context_summary: Born in Flums, Switzerland. Family background not documented in reviewed sources beyond her membership in the Skiclub Flumserberg.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Swiss alpine skiing pipeline, Skiclub Flumserberg, Swiss Alps geography, junior national champion, Olympic gold at 17
evidence_summary: Nadig's early success was built on the Swiss alpine skiing pipeline: growing up in Flums near the Flumserberg ski area, joining the local ski club, and rising through junior national championships to the World Cup circuit. The Swiss Alps provided a native skiing environment, and the national skiing infrastructure supported her development. At 17, she defeated the world's best to win two Olympic golds, a feat recognized with Swiss Sportswoman of the Year. Family financial or domain background is not documented.
starting_point: Born in 1954 in Flums, Switzerland, in the Alps near the Flumserberg ski area; family background not documented beyond local ski club membership.
current_position: Retired alpine skier with 24 World Cup wins and 57 podium finishes; operated a sports store and hotel in Switzerland after retirement; served as national ski coach from 1999 to 2005.

trajectory.event: Won the giant slalom at the Swiss Junior National Championships, her first major competition.
Won two Olympic gold medals (downhill and giant slalom) at the Sapporo Winter Olympics, defeating favorite Annemarie Moser-Pröll; named Swiss Sportswoman of the Year.
Won Olympic bronze in downhill at the Lake Placid Olympics after a dominant World Cup season.
Won the overall World Cup title and retired from competition with 24 World Cup victories.
Became a national ski coach for Switzerland, serving until 2005.

name: Rodion Shchedrin
milestone_by_age_26: Premiered his First Piano Concerto as soloist in 1954 at age 22 while still a student at the Moscow Conservatory, and had his ballet 'The Little Humpbacked Horse' premiered in 1955 at age 23, which became a staple of the Bolshoi Ballet repertoire.
early_history_summary: Shchedrin was born in Moscow into a musical family: his father was a composer and music theory teacher, and his mother worked in the financial planning department at the Bolshoi Theatre. He studied at the Moscow Choral School and then the Moscow Conservatory under Yuri Shaporin (composition) and Yakov Flier (piano), graduating in 1955. His early works incorporated Russian folk music, and he led a 1951 expedition to Belarus to collect folk songs.
family_context_summary: Born in Moscow to a musical family: father was a composer and music theory teacher, mother worked at the Bolshoi Theatre in financial planning. His grandfather was an Orthodox priest whose village folk tales inspired much of Shchedrin's music.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a composer and teacher of music theory; mother worked at the Bolshoi Theatre. The family provided direct musical mentorship and institutional connections to the Bolshoi.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father composer and music theory teacher, mother at Bolshoi Theatre, Moscow Conservatory, Yuri Shaporin, Yakov Flier, Bolshoi Ballet premiere, Russian folk music
evidence_summary: Shchedrin's early advantage was exceptional: his father was a composer and music theory teacher, and his mother worked at the Bolshoi Theatre, providing both domain mentorship and institutional connections. He trained at the elite Moscow Choral School and Moscow Conservatory under renowned teachers Yuri Shaporin and Yakov Flier. By 22, he performed his own piano concerto; by 23, his ballet premiered at the Bolshoi. The Soviet state arts system provided financial support and a platform for his compositions.
starting_point: Born in 1932 in Moscow into a musical family; father was a composer and music theory teacher, mother worked at the Bolshoi Theatre, grandfather was an Orthodox priest.
current_position: Died on August 29, 2025 in Munich at age 92; regarded as one of the leading composers of the late Soviet period; final works included operas and ballets performed internationally.

trajectory.event: Performed the solo part of his First Piano Concerto with Gennady Rozhdestvensky conducting, while still a student at the Moscow Conservatory.
Ballet 'The Little Humpbacked Horse' premiered and became a staple of the Bolshoi Ballet; graduated from the Moscow Conservatory.
Married ballerina Maya Plisetskaya of the Bolshoi Theatre, beginning a lifelong personal and artistic partnership.
Opera 'Not Love Alone' premiered, consolidating his reputation as a major Soviet composer.
Began teaching composition at the Moscow Conservatory, a position he held until 1969.
Composed the Carmen Suite for Maya Plisetskaya, one of his most internationally performed works.
Died on August 29 in Munich, Germany.

name: Anthony Fauci
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Fauci graduated with an MD from Cornell University Medical College in 1966 at age 26 (top of class), but his major career milestones—joining NIH in 1968, becoming lab chief, directing NIAID in 1984, and HIV/AIDS research breakthroughs—all came after age 26.
early_history_summary: Fauci was born in Brooklyn, New York, and attended Regis High School in Manhattan. He graduated from the College of the Holy Cross in 1962 with a BA in pre-medicine and earned his MD from Cornell University Medical College in 1966, finishing at the top of his class. He then began a four-year internship and residency at New York Hospital-Cornell Medical Center before joining the NIH in 1968.
family_context_summary: Born in Brooklyn, New York. Father Stephen Fauci was a pharmacist who owned his own pharmacy in Bensonhurst; the family lived above the pharmacy. Mother Eugenia Fauci attended Brooklyn College and Hunter College. Both sets of grandparents were Italian immigrants.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a pharmacist who owned his own pharmacy; young Fauci helped deliver prescriptions by bicycle. This provided some exposure to healthcare but not directly to biomedical research.
evidence_summary: Fauci's early path was conventional: a strong education at Regis High School, Holy Cross, and Cornell Medical College, graduating at the top of his class at 26. His father's pharmacy provided modest healthcare exposure. All major career milestones—joining NIH (1968), heading the Clinical Physiology Section (1974), directing NIAID (1984), HIV/AIDS breakthroughs, and COVID-19 leadership—came well after age 26. Medical school graduation alone does not constitute a material milestone under the rubric.

name: Alfred Brendel
milestone_by_age_26: Won fourth prize at the Ferruccio Busoni Piano Competition in 1949 at age 18, made his first recording (Prokofiev Piano Concerto No. 5) in 1950 at 19, and made the world premiere recording of Liszt's Weihnachtsbaum in 1952 at 21, establishing an international performing and recording career.
early_history_summary: Brendel was born in Vizmberk, Czechoslovakia, to a non-musical family. He moved to Zagreb at age three and began piano lessons at six with Sofija Deželić. The family later moved to Graz, Austria, where he studied at the Graz Conservatory with Ludovica von Kaan. He was largely self-taught after age 16, gave his first public recital at 17 in Graz, and won the Busoni Competition prize at 18, launching his career.
family_context_summary: Born to a non-musical family in Vizmberk, Czechoslovakia. Father worked as an architectural engineer, businessman, resort hotel manager, and cinema director. The family moved frequently between Yugoslavia and Austria. There was no music in the household.
parent_family_domain_summary: No musical family background. Father had various non-musical professions. Brendel explicitly stated he was not a child prodigy and his parents were not musicians.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Graz Conservatory, Busoni Competition, self-taught after 16, early recordings, Edwin Fischer master classes, wartime displacement
evidence_summary: Brendel's early career was remarkably self-driven: born to a non-musical family with no inherited musical advantages, he was largely self-taught after age 16. His early milestones—the Busoni Competition prize at 18, first recording at 19, and world premiere recording at 21—were achieved through intense self-directed study and concentration. The Graz Conservatory provided foundational training, and master classes with Edwin Fischer offered crucial mentorship. WWII disrupted his childhood, sending him to dig trenches at 14, which may have contributed to his independent, self-reliant approach.
starting_point: Born in 1931 in Vizmberk, Czechoslovakia, to a non-musical family; father was an architectural engineer, businessman, and cinema director; family moved between Yugoslavia and Austria during Brendel's childhood.
current_position: Died on June 17, 2025 in London at age 94; regarded as one of the greatest pianists of the 20th century, noted for Beethoven, Schubert, and Liszt interpretations; first pianist to record Beethoven's complete solo piano works.

trajectory.event: Gave his first public recital in Graz, titled 'The Fugue in Piano Literature,' including a self-composed piano sonata.
Won fourth prize at the Ferruccio Busoni Piano Competition in Bolzano, Italy, launching his professional career.
Made his first recording, Prokofiev's Piano Concerto No. 5.
Made the world premiere recording of Liszt's Weihnachtsbaum.
Moved to Hampstead, London, where he lived for the rest of his life.
International breakthrough after a Beethoven recital at the Queen Elizabeth Hall in London; three major record labels contacted his agent the next day.
Died on June 17 in London, England.

name: Sergey Volkov
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Volkov qualified as a test cosmonaut in November 1999 at age 26, but this was a training completion rather than a material achievement. His first spaceflight did not occur until April 2008 at age 35 aboard Soyuz TMA-12.
early_history_summary: Volkov was born in Chuhuiv, Kharkiv Oblast, Ukraine, the son of cosmonaut Aleksandr Volkov. He grew up in Star City (Zvyozdny Gorodok), graduated from Star City High School in 1990, and entered the Tambov Air Force Academy for Pilots, graduating in 1995 as a pilot-engineer. He served in the Russian Air Force before being selected as a cosmonaut candidate in 1997.
family_context_summary: Born in Chuhuiv, Ukraine, the son of cosmonaut Aleksandr Volkov. He grew up in Star City (Zvyozdny Gorodok), the cosmonaut training center, and became the first second-generation cosmonaut.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Aleksandr Volkov was a cosmonaut, providing direct domain exposure and unique access to the cosmonaut training environment. Sergey grew up in Star City surrounded by the cosmonaut community.
evidence_summary: Volkov had extraordinary inherited access as the son of cosmonaut Aleksandr Volkov, growing up in Star City. However, his actual material milestone—first spaceflight in 2008 at age 35—came well after age 26. Completing cosmonaut training by 26 is a career step, not a material achievement under the rubric. His father's cosmonaut career provided domain proximity but did not translate to a verifiable milestone by 26.
